claims.claim: A software library was built and published that implements the method developed in Victor and Conte, 2012 for generating structured textures.
claims.source: To generate these textures we built and published a software library (Piasini, 2021) that implements the method developed in Victor and Conte, 2012.
claims.evidence: This describes a methodological contribution with citations to the original method and the new implementation.

claims.claim: For any given type of multipoint correlation, textures were sampled from the distribution over binary textures that had the desired probability of occurrence of that statistic but otherwise contained the least amount of structure (maximum entropy).
claims.source: Briefly, for any given type of multipoint correlation (also termed a statistic in what follows), we sampled from the distribution over binary textures that had the desired probability of occurrence of that statistic, but otherwise contained the least amount of structure (i.e. had maximum entropy).
claims.evidence: This describes the method for generating textures based on Victor and Conte, 2012.

claims.claim: The probability of occurrence of the pattern was parametrized by the intensity of the corresponding statistic, determined by a parity count of white or black pixels inside tiles of 1, 2, 3, or 4 pixels (termed gliders).
claims.source: The probability of occurrence of the pattern was parametrized by the intensity of the corresponding statistic, determined by a parity count of white or black pixels inside tiles of 1, 2, 3, or 4 pixels (termed gliders) used as the building blocks of the texture (Victor and Conte, 2012).
claims.evidence: This describes the parametrization method with citation to the original work.

claims.claim: When the intensity is zero, the texture does not contain any structure and is the same as white noise.
claims.source: When the intensity is zero, the texture does not contain any structure–it is the same as white noise (Figure 1A, left).
claims.evidence: This describes a property of the stimulus generation method and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: When the intensity is +1, every possible placement of the glider across the texture contains an even number of white pixels.
claims.source: When the intensity is +1, every possible placement of the glider across the texture contains an even number of white pixels, while a level of –1 corresponds to all placements containing an odd number of white pixels.
claims.evidence: This describes a property of the stimulus generation method.

claims.claim: When the intensity is -1, all placements of the glider contain an odd number of white pixels.
claims.source: When the intensity is +1, every possible placement of the glider across the texture contains an even number of white pixels, while a level of –1 corresponds to all placements containing an odd number of white pixels.
claims.evidence: This describes a property of the stimulus generation method.

claims.claim: Intermediate intensity levels correspond to intermediate fractions of gliders containing the even parity count.
claims.source: Intermediate intensity levels correspond to intermediate fractions of gliders containing the even parity count.
claims.evidence: This describes a property of the stimulus generation method.

claims.claim: For positive intensity levels, a one-point glider produces textures with increasingly large luminance.
claims.source: For instance (see examples in Figure 1A, right), for positive intensity levels, a one-point glider produces textures with increasingly large luminance, a two-point glider produces oriented edges and a four-point glider produces rectangular blocks.

claims.claim: For positive intensity levels, a two-point glider produces oriented edges.

claims.claim: For positive intensity levels, a four-point glider produces rectangular blocks.

claims.claim: A three-point glider produces L-shape patterns, either black or white depending on whether the intensity is negative or positive.

claims.claim: Two-point and three-point gliders are associated to multiple distinct multipoint correlations, corresponding to different spatial glider configurations.
claims.source: Notably, two-point and three-point gliders are associated to multiple distinct multipoint correlations, corresponding to different spatial glider configurations.
claims.evidence: This describes a property of the texture statistics based on the method from Victor and Conte, 2012.

claims.claim: In the previous study with human participants, all two-point, three-point, and four-point configurations were tested, as well as 11 of their pairwise combinations, for a total of 20 different texture statistics.
claims.source: In our previous study with human participants (Hermundstad et al., 2014), we tested all these two-point, three-point, and four-point configurations, as well as 11 of their pairwise combinations, for a total of 20 different texture statistics.
claims.evidence: This describes the scope of the previous human study with citation.

claims.claim: Textures defined by one-point correlations were not tested in the previous human study because the method used to measure variability of texture statistics across natural images could not be applied to the one-point statistic.
claims.source: In that set of experiments, we did not test textures defined by one-point correlations because, by construction, the method we used to measure the variability of texture statistics across natural images could not be applied to the one-point statistic.
claims.evidence: This explains a methodological limitation of the previous study.

claims.claim: Practical and ethical constraints prevented measuring rat sensitivity to a large number of statistic combinations because a different group of animals had to be trained with each tested statistic.
claims.source: In our current study, practical and ethical constraints prevented us from measuring rat sensitivity to a large number of statistic combinations, because a different group of animals had to be trained with each tested statistic (see below), meaning that the number of rats required for the experiments increased rapidly with the number of statistics studied.
claims.evidence: This explains the experimental design constraints of the current study.

claims.claim: The 4-point statistic was chosen for testing in rats.
claims.source: Therefore, we chose to test the 4-point statistic, as well as one each of the two-point and three-point statistics (those shown in Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design choice.

claims.claim: The one-point statistic was tested because rat visual system sensitivity to luminance changes is well-established and performance with this statistic served as a useful benchmark.
claims.source: In addition, we also tested the one-point statistic because, given the well-established sensitivity of the rat visual system to luminance changes (Minini and Jeffery, 2006; Tafazoli et al., 2017; Vascon et al., 2019; Vermaercke and Op de Beeck, 2012), performance with this statistic served as a useful benchmark against which to compare rat discrimination of the other, more complex textures.
claims.evidence: This explains the rationale for including one-point statistics with citations to previous work on rat vision.

claims.claim: The rat visual system has well-established sensitivity to luminance changes.

claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies on rat vision.

claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design of the current study.

claims.claim: Each trial started with the rat autonomously triggering stimulus presentation by licking the central response port.

claims.evidence: This describes the behavioral task procedure.

claims.source: The rat received liquid reward for correct choices and was subjected to a time-out period for incorrect ones (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This describes the reinforcement schedule used in the behavioral task.

claims.claim: In the initial phase of the experiment, the intensity of the statistic was set to a single level close to the maximum (or minimum for three-point) to make discrimination as easy as possible for naive rats.
claims.source: In the initial phase of the experiment, the intensity of the statistic was set to a single level, close to the maximum (or minimum, in case of the three-point statistic, for which we used only negative values), to make the discrimination between structured textures and white noise as easy as possible for naive rats that had to learn the task from scratch.

claims.evidence: This is quantitative data from the learning phase of the experiment.

claims.claim: Animals trained on two-point correlations required on average 5.3 ± 1.3 blocks of 500 trials to reach criterion (n = 8).
claims.source: Specifically, considering only those rats that reached criterion performance, animals trained on one-point correlations required on average 3.5 ± 0.3 blocks of 500 trials (n = 9) to reach criterion; those trained on two-point correlations 5.3 ± 1.3 (n = 8); those trained on 3-point statistic 3.4 ± 1.6 (n = 5); and those trained on four-point correlations 11.8 ± 1.6 (n = 10).
claims.evidence: This is quantitative data from the learning phase of the experiment.

claims.claim: Animals trained on three-point correlations required on average 3.4 ± 1.6 blocks of 500 trials to reach criterion (n = 5).

claims.evidence: This is quantitative data from the learning phase of the experiment.

claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from within-subject comparisons.

results.result: Four groups of rats (n=42 total, with 9-12 per group) were trained in a visual texture discrimination task to distinguish white noise from structured textures containing one of four multipoint correlation statistics (1-, 2-, 3-, or 4-point). The experimental design included multiple training phases with adaptive difficulty adjustment, followed by psychometric testing across a range of intensity levels. Stimuli were maximum-entropy binary textures generated using established methods, displayed on calibrated monitors with pixel sizes appropriate for rat visual acuity.
results.evaluation: The experimental design and methods are thoroughly documented with appropriate technical details (C3, C18-C31, C46-C49, C110-C160). The stimulus generation method is properly cited and implemented (C21-C23), display parameters are calibrated and justified based on rat visual capabilities (C122-C129), and the behavioral paradigm is clearly described with appropriate controls for bias and learning (C130-C160). Sample sizes are reasonable for psychophysical studies and attrition is documented (C119-C120, C137-C138).

results.result: During initial training (Phase I), rats trained on different statistics showed differential learning rates. Animals trained on 1- and 2-point statistics reached criterion performance (65% correct over 500 trials) faster (3.5±0.3 and 5.3±1.3 blocks, respectively) than those trained on 3-point (3.4±1.6 blocks) and 4-point statistics (11.8±1.6 blocks).
results.evaluation: The learning data (C50-C54) are quantitative and include sample sizes and error estimates. The differential learning rates align with the later sensitivity findings, providing convergent evidence. However, the 3-point learning rate appears inconsistent with the pattern (faster than 2-point despite lower final sensitivity), which may warrant discussion but doesn't invalidate the overall finding.

results.result: Rat perceptual sensitivity to multipoint statistics, measured using an ideal observer model fitted to psychometric data, showed a clear ranking: 2-point horizontal > 4-point > 3-point correlations. This ranking matches both the sensitivity observed in humans and the variability of these statistics across natural images.
results.evaluation: The main result is supported by psychometric data analyzed with an appropriate ideal observer model (C58, C60-C62). The sensitivity ranking (C4, C67) is statistically significant (Figure 2C shows p<0.01 to p<0.001 for pairwise comparisons) and replicates the human pattern (C66). The model provides interpretable parameters (1/σ as sensitivity) with clear theoretical justification (C60-C61).

results.result: The quantitative values of rat sensitivity matched human sensitivity and natural image statistics up to a scaling factor, with degree of correspondence values of 0.990 (rat vs. human, p=0.05) and 0.986 (rat vs. image statistics, p=0.07). These values are comparable to those reported for human-image correspondence (0.987-0.999) in the prior study.
results.evaluation: While the degree of correspondence values are high (C69-C70), the statistical significance is marginal, particularly for the rat-image comparison (p=0.07, C69). The comparison is based on only three data points (2-, 3-, and 4-point statistics), which limits statistical power. The Monte Carlo test is appropriate, but the borderline significance and small sample size make this quantitative claim less certain than the qualitative ranking. Additional statistics would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: Generalization testing (Phase IV) revealed that the sensitivity ranking is robust and independent of training history. Rats trained on 1- or 2-point statistics performed poorly when switched to 3- or 4-point statistics, while rats trained on 4-point performed well on 2-point. Critically, 4-point sensitivity exceeded 3-point sensitivity across all groups tested, regardless of which statistic they were originally trained on.
results.evaluation: The generalization results (C73-C76, C161-C165) provide strong within-subject and cross-group validation of the sensitivity ranking. The asymmetric transfer (easy-to-hard fails, hard-to-easy succeeds) is consistent with genuine perceptual limitations rather than task-specific learning. The design is well-controlled with appropriate group assignments (C162-C165).

results.result: Within-subject comparisons confirmed that 4-point sensitivity is statistically higher than 3-point sensitivity. This held both for rats trained on 4-point and tested on 3-point (p<0.01, paired t-test) and, critically, for rats trained on 3-point and tested on 4-point (p<0.05, paired t-test).
results.evaluation: The within-subject statistical tests (C77-C78) provide the strongest evidence for the 4-point > 3-point ranking, as they control for individual differences. The fact that this holds even when rats were extensively trained on 3-point (C78) is particularly compelling. The use of paired one-tailed t-tests is appropriate given the directional hypothesis. This addresses a key prediction of efficient coding theory (C82-C83).

results.result: The study demonstrates that rat sensitivity to multipoint texture statistics reproduces the pattern observed in humans, providing evidence that rodents and humans are similarly adapted to process visual texture statistics in accordance with efficient coding principles.
results.evaluation: This conclusion is well-supported by the convergence of multiple lines of evidence: the qualitative sensitivity ranking matches humans (C5, C80-C81), the quantitative correspondence is high (C84), the pattern holds across different experimental manipulations (within-subject, cross-group), and it aligns with natural image statistics. The claim is appropriately scoped to the tested statistics (C107).

results.result: The experimental design choices (testing only 3 of the statistics from the human study, using only one polarity per statistic, selecting specific glider configurations) were justified by practical/ethical constraints and the need to adapt stimuli to rat visual capabilities while avoiding confounds from low acuity and OFF-response dominance.
results.evaluation: The rationale for design choices is thoroughly documented (C37, C85-C106). The selection of statistics was strategic to maximize discriminability of the efficient coding signature (C85-C88). The polarity choices are well-justified based on rat visual physiology (C89-C103) and prior human data showing polarity-independence (C104). While these choices limit the scope of comparison with humans, they are appropriate given the constraints and do not undermine the main conclusions.

results.result: A control analysis excluding rats from the second batch that did not reach 65% criterion in Phase I training confirmed that the sensitivity ranking and statistical significance of pairwise comparisons were unchanged.
results.evaluation: This is an important control (C149) that addresses a potential selection bias concern (C147). The fact that results are unchanged when excluding potentially poor performers strengthens confidence that the findings reflect typical rat sensitivity rather than being driven by exceptional animals. The reasoning for this analysis is sound (C147-C148).

results.result: The findings establish rats as a suitable model for studying efficient coding of visual textures, opening possibilities for causal investigations through optogenetic or controlled-rearing experiments that are not feasible in humans or primates.
results.evaluation: This conclusion appropriately synthesizes the background literature (C1-C2, C6-C17) with the current findings to identify future research directions (C108-C109). The rationale for using rodents (experimental tractability, C12-C16) combined with the demonstration of similar perceptual organization to humans provides solid justification for this model system. The claim is appropriately framed as enabling future work rather than as a direct finding of the current study.

results.result: Two-point and three-point gliders correspond to multiple distinct spatial configurations. The previous human study tested all configurations plus pairwise combinations (20 statistics total), but did not test one-point correlations due to methodological constraints in measuring natural image variability.
results.evaluation: These claims accurately describe properties of the stimulus space (C32) and the scope of prior work (C35-C36). The explanation for omitting one-point statistics in the human study is methodologically sound (C36). This provides important context for comparing the current rat study to prior human work.

results.result: Key properties of rat vision relevant to stimulus design include: well-established sensitivity to luminance changes, much lower visual acuity than humans (~1 cycle/degree maximum resolution), and dominance of OFF over ON responses in central vision.
results.evaluation: These claims about rat visual capabilities are well-supported by citations to multiple prior studies (C43, C90, C92, C99-C101, C125). The acuity value is consistently cited across multiple sources. These properties appropriately informed stimulus design decisions (pixel size, polarity choices).

results.result: Sample size (n=42 rats total, ~10 per statistic) was determined by statistical needs and rig capacity constraints. Two batches were tested (2018-2019 and 2019-2020), with documented attrition due to failure to reach criterion or death. All procedures were approved by Italian authorities.
results.evaluation: The sample size justification is reasonable (C115-C116), the timeline is documented (C117-C118), attrition is transparently reported (C119-C120), and ethical approval is documented (C121). The sample sizes per group (8-11 animals reaching final testing) are adequate for psychophysical studies, though larger samples would increase power for the quantitative correspondence analyses.
